hook: The two-task rule. Here's exactly how it works.
topic: The two-task rule — simplifying daily priority architecture
body:
**The two-task rule. Here's exactly how it works.**

At the start of every day, you identify two outputs — not tasks, outputs. Something that will exist at the end of the day that didn't exist at the start. Not "work on the presentation." The first three slides of the presentation, finished.

Only two. Not five, not ten. Two. Because the human brain is genuinely capable of reliably achieving two meaningful outputs per day. Ten tasks gives you ten ways to feel like you're making progress while avoiding the two things that actually matter.

Once those two outputs are identified, they are non-negotiable. Everything else — email, meetings, admin, other people's priorities — happens in the space around them. Not instead of them.

The rule works because it removes the daily negotiation about what to prioritise. That negotiation is where avoidance gets its foothold. When the question is already answered before the day starts, there's nothing left to negotiate.

The reframe: you don't need to do more. You need to stop letting everything else replace the two things that matter.

One action: tonight, write two specific outputs for tomorrow. Not intentions. Specific, completeable things. Put them somewhere you'll see before you open anything else.

Full system in the link in bio.
visual_direction: Kai Ren standing. Hold up two fingers briefly when stating "only two" — not theatrical, just a clean visual anchor. Confident and simple.
text_overlay: "Two outputs. Not tasks — outputs. That's the whole rule."
caption_hook: You don't need a better to-do list. You need to stop putting ten things on it. The two-task rule.
